findings.title: The proposed backend seam is much broader than five platform operations
findings.body: [cost] Established from `terminal.rs:227-257,336-1061`: `Terminal` combines platform handles with 24 public behaviors covering wakeups, event polling, resizing, rendering, capability probes, colors, pointer shape, and clipboard operations; `engine/mod.rs`, `engine/clipboard.rs`, `engine/doc.rs`, `native.rs`, and `pixel-node/src/lib.rs` call that concrete API directly. Therefore Task 2 either preserves `Terminal` as a substantial common facade over low-level backends or expands the trait and changes those callers, and every future terminal capability must then be maintained and tested across both Unix and Windows. That price is justified only if retaining the compositor and browser chrome saves more than the permanent two-backend compatibility surface. This point is overturned by an explicit facade design that confines `TerminalBackend` to low-level byte I/O, waiting, sizing, and presentation while demonstrably leaving the public `Terminal` contract and callers unchanged.

findings.title: Windows requires porting two existing Unix-socket protocols, not only the new control-pipe client
findings.body: [cost] Established from `store/src/paths.ts:46-48`, `browser/src/daemon.ts:38-39,66,152-157`, and `browser/src/registry.ts:52-57`: upstream has a daemon Unix-domain socket and a separate per-browser socket, both represented as filesystem paths and deleted with `fs.rmSync`. Their endpoint strings are also stored in the instances database (`store/src/schema.ts:7`) and consumed by `cli/src/main.ts`, `control.ts`, `instances.ts`, and `action.ts`. Porting them to Windows named pipes therefore reaches path policy, two servers, all clients, stale-endpoint cleanup, persisted instance records, and lifecycle tests; it also creates a permanent endpoint-naming contract distinct from the agwinterm frame pipe. The price is warranted if the multiprocess daemon and per-instance CLI-control model are required on Windows. This point is overturned if Task 11 supplies and tests one shared endpoint abstraction covering both protocols, every listed consumer, persistence, and cleanup.

findings.title: A Windows build, launch, and distribution pipeline is additional unbudgeted work
findings.body: [cost] Established: the native build helper treats every non-macOS target as `libpixel_node.so` (`build-native.mjs:9`), `browser/package.json:7-10` invokes Bash and `exec`, and `cli/src/main.ts:61-109` assumes Unix Electron names, shell quoting, `/bin/sh`, and Unix stderr redirection. Task 6's Rust match-arm work cannot by itself produce a loadable `pixel.node`, and a runnable port also needs Windows-specific Electron discovery and process/log launching; an installable port additionally needs replacements for the deliberately unvendored Unix release and installer scripts. This is an ongoing cost because Electron layout, N-API artifacts, development launch, and release packaging must remain synchronized. The value must include a reproducible Windows runtime or installation, not merely a compiling Rust workspace, for that price to be justified. This point is overturned if a Windows-native build/launcher/packager already exists outside the searched upstream tree and is explicitly adopted by the plan.

findings.title: Preserving CLI pane integration expands the agwinterm-side scope
findings.body: [cost] Established: `pixel-terminals` has no agwinterm detector (`terminals/src/terminals/index.ts:15-25`), while its `split` contract requires opening a directional pane and running a supplied command, and `cli/src/main.ts:402-404` depends on that contract. agwinterm's current control API exposes `session.new` with a command but `session.split` accepts only an operation (`../agwinterm/src/Agwinterm.Pty/ControlServer.cs:134-135,163`), so matching upstream `--split` semantics requires either multi-command discovery/targeting orchestration or another agwinterm contract change beyond the `image.frameshm` dependency plan. That adds a host adapter, pane-identity and direction mapping, failure cleanup, and cross-repository tests; it is worth paying only if agent-driven split placement and current-tab browser discovery are part of the Windows product value. This point is overturned by a documented existing agwinterm command sequence that atomically returns the new pane identity and runs the requested command with direction and size semantics.

findings.title: One supposedly unchanged pixel-core module needs Windows path work
findings.body: [cost] Established from `clipboard_image.rs:78-98`: pasted image paths are accepted only when they begin with `/` or `~`, and home expansion reads `HOME`; a normal `C:\...` path is rejected before `PathBuf` is consulted. The existing tests at lines 142-171 also feed native temporary paths back through this parser, so this module and its tests cannot remain unchanged on Windows. The reach is small—one parser plus platform cases—and does not materially undermine retaining `pixel-core`; supporting pasted local images is enough value to justify it. This point is overturned if every Windows paste reaching `Engine` is independently normalized to a slash-prefixed file URL before `image_path_from_paste` is called.

findings.title: The module the brief writes off as a rewrite is ~25% portable VT decoder, already tested — and it is exactly what Task 3 needs
findings.body:
You asked whether the reference-count proxy fails. It does fail, and on this axis it fails in the plan's favour. I re-ran the count per file and reproduced 64/2/2 with 19 zeros exactly. But I then listed the line numbers of every unix hit inside terminal.rs, and they stop at 1250 and do not resume until 1956 — and 1910 is where the first `#[cfg(test)]` module begins. Established: lines 1251–1909 of terminal.rs, roughly 660 lines of production code, contain zero references to rustix, std::os::unix, termios, libc or /dev/tty. What lives there is the entire VT input decoder: `parse_event_kitty` (1337), `parse_plain_bytes` (1383), `byte_key_event` (1430), `parse_csi` (1452), `parse_kitty_key` (1630), `parse_sgr_mouse` (1771), `parse_kitty_keyboard` (1811), `parse_osc_color` (1860), plus the bracketed-paste and clipboard-packet parsers. These are pure byte-slice functions.

What follows from that: Task 3's hardest-sounding checkbox — 'decode SGR mouse reports (?1006) and kitty keyboard sequences' — is not work to be done, it is work to be linked against. The plan already half-knows this ('feed the bytes to the existing VT input decoder rather than writing a second decoder') but the brief's 64-hit accounting hides how much of terminal.rs that decoder is, so the cost line for 'replace one module' is materially overstated.

The test position is stronger still. The test module at 1910 holds 29 tests; enumerating their names, at least 25 are pure byte-sequence parser tests — `parses_sgr_mouse_events`, `sgr_mouse_decodes_modifier_bits`, `parses_modifiers_on_legacy_and_kitty_keys`, `parses_kitty_repeat_and_release_events`, `parses_kitty_associated_text_and_function_keys`, `ctrl_bytes_and_alt_prefixes_decode_as_modified_chars`, `utf8_input_decodes_whole_chars`, `bracketed_paste_arrives_as_one_normalized_event`, and `parse_event_consumes_one_event_and_reports_incomplete_tails`. That last one is literally the 'a sequence split across two reads' case Task 3 lists as a test to be written. Only `shm_roundtrip` (1951) and `a_frame_file_is_rewritten_in_place_and_removed_on_drop` in that module are unix-bound; the 4 tests in `tty_tests` (2480+) are openpty-based and separate.

This bears on your stated fear about autonomous execution more than on cost. The riskiest thing about Windows console input is not calling SetConsoleMode — it is decoding kitty keyboard and SGR mouse correctly, where a subtle error produces plausible-looking wrong input that no milestone screenshot catches. That component arrives pre-written and pre-verified against ~25 recorded-byte tests that run unchanged on Windows.

What would overturn it: if the decoder functions turn out to take fd-typed or Termios-typed arguments from their callers rather than plain byte slices, the reuse would need more shimming than I am claiming. I read the signatures of `parse_csi`, `parse_sgr_mouse` and `parse_event_kitty` and they take `&[u8]`, but I did not trace every caller in the 1251–1909 range.

findings.title: Task 8 needs no agwinterm change at all, and its workload sits inside the already-shipping envelope of image.frame
findings.body:
This is your question 3 and question 4, and they answer together. I read agwinterm's `HandleImageFrame` at `src/Agwinterm.Pty/ControlServer.cs:426` in full. Established, not inferred: it takes `args.images[]`; each entry supplies `path`, `row`, `col`, `cols`, `rows` and optional source crop; it computes a `ContentSignature` from mtime/length/path and skips the file read when the id's signature is unchanged; phase 1 reads the bytes off the render lock and phase 2 takes `MutateLocked` only for `ClearPlacements` + `SetImageData(id, KittyFormat.Png, 0, 0, data)` + `PlaceImage(...)`. Every capability Task 5 asks for — cell-span scaling via cols/rows, id reuse against the content cache — is present in shipped code, and the dispatch entry is at line 249 exactly as the brief cites.

What follows: Tasks 1–8 have zero dependency on the agwinterm plan. The entire cross-repo contract risk is confined to Task 10, which is an optimization, and the plan already makes Task 10 self-guarding — its precondition bullet says stop rather than guess the layout, and it requires automatic fallback. I checked that the fallback is implementable against a real string rather than an assumed one: `ControlServer.cs:523` is `Err(string error) => {"ok":false,"error":<json>}` and the dispatch default at line 250 is `Err($"unknown command '{cmd}'")`. So Task 10's test 'the fallback triggers on an {"ok":false,"error":"unknown command..."} reply' is written against text that exists today.

And the milestone's workload is inside the proven envelope. agwinterm's own gap analysis (`docs/agterm-gap-analysis.md:41`) records that the file-based control-pipe path is the shipping Kitty-graphics route, used by docxy; agwinterm's design spec (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-06-30-agwinterm-design.md:204`) records that docxy emits static images. Task 8's deliverable is 'a static page legibly on screen' — a static image, which is precisely the workload image.frame is already in production for. The performance question that motivates shm is the *animated* case, and Task 8 is correctly placed to produce the measurement that justifies it rather than assuming it.

What would overturn it: if a full-pane 1920x1080 PNG encode plus file write plus agwinterm's PNG decode is slow enough that even a single static page takes seconds to appear, Task 8 would stall on a performance problem it was not scoped to solve. I could not measure this — measuring means running a build, which is outside this review — and the number does not exist yet on either side; the agwinterm plan's Task 6 is where it gets produced.

findings.title: Both portability risks you named by hand — arboard and fontdue — resolve clean, and the font path has no system dependency at all
findings.body:
You flagged arboard and fontdue specifically as places the zero-hit column might be lying. I checked both against the actual crate manifests in the local cargo registry rather than reasoning from reputation.

arboard 3.6.1: its Cargo.toml declares `[target."cfg(windows)".dependencies.clipboard-win]` and `windows-sys`, i.e. a first-class Windows backend. The feature the workspace enables, `wayland-data-control`, maps to the optional `wl-clipboard-rs`, which is declared under `[target.'cfg(all(unix, not(any(target_os="macos", target_os="android", target_os="emscripten"))))'.dependencies]` — a target-gated optional dependency is not built for a non-matching target, so enabling that feature on Windows pulls nothing in. Established separately: pixel-core has exactly one arboard call site, `clipboard_image.rs:56`, and it is `arboard::Clipboard::new().ok()?` — so even a runtime failure to open the clipboard degrades to `None` rather than a panic or a build break.

fontdue 0.9.3: no `[target.…]` sections at all; its only non-optional dependency is `ttf-parser` with default features off. Pure Rust rasterizer, nothing to port.

The font concern resolves harder than 'portable'. I grepped pixel-core for font acquisition and every hit is `include_bytes!("../../../assets/fonts/JetBrainsMono-Regular.ttf")` — menu.rs:356, paint.rs:775, text_input.rs:917, wrap.rs:139, tree/tests.rs:8. There is no system font enumeration, no fontconfig, no CoreText, no DirectWrite call anywhere in the crate; the typeface is compiled in. That also means the test fixtures are self-contained, which is what makes the regression net portable.

What would overturn it: a build is the only real proof, and I did not run one. Specifically, cargo's handling of a feature that names a target-gated optional dependency is what my arboard conclusion rests on; if the workspace's feature unification pulled `wl-clipboard-rs` in on a Windows target anyway, that crate would fail to build. The 41-error baseline you already measured is the evidence against that worry — those errors are in pixel-core's own source, not in a dependency.

findings.title: Task 2's real deliverable buys a live 200-test tripwire for exactly the failure mode you are afraid of
findings.body:
Your standard is that a wrong assumption becomes a long autonomous run that builds the wrong thing and looks like it succeeded. The strongest structural argument for this plan's ordering is that Task 2 is placed to defeat that specific failure mode, and the plan says so almost in passing — its bullet 'verify cargo check --workspace is clean on Windows — this is the task's real deliverable'.

Established by counting: pixel-core carries 252 `#[test]` functions across 29 source files. Of those, 33 are in terminal.rs, 12 in herdr.rs and 4 in ghostty.rs, so roughly 203 live in the modules the plan promises not to touch, and their fixtures are compiled-in fonts rather than system resources.

What follows: today those 203 tests cannot run on Windows at all, because lib.rs (lines 1–26) declares `mod terminal`, `mod herdr` and `pub mod ghostty` unconditionally, so the crate does not compile and nothing downstream of it is verifiable. The moment Task 2 lands the cfg gates, all 203 become a per-task regression net that runs on every subsequent task's 'tests must pass before Task N+1' gate. That converts the plan's central promise — nineteen modules unchanged — from an intention into something mechanically checked eleven times, and Task 12's `git diff` against the vendored baseline closes the loop on changes the tests would not catch.

This is also why Task 2's position before Tasks 3–7 is not arbitrary sequencing: every later task is being executed against a compiler and a test suite that work, rather than against a crate that cannot build. For autonomous execution that is the difference between a task that fails loudly and a task that produces plausible untested code.

What would overturn it: if a meaningful share of those 203 tests turn out to depend transitively on terminal.rs's `Terminal` struct rather than on its plain types, they would be cfg-gated off alongside it and the net would be thinner than the count suggests. I confirmed the coupling is mostly type-level (see the module-count finding) but did not compile the test tree to see how many survive gating.

findings.title: The brief undercounts its own evidence: the portable surface is 43 of 46 files, not 19 of 22
findings.body:
The '19 of 22 modules' row is the single piece of evidence the whole architectural bet rests on, so it is worth knowing that it is counted conservatively. Established: the 22 figure counts only top-level `.rs` files in `pixel-core/src`. There are five subdirectories — `engine/`, `scroll/`, `selection/`, `surfaces/`, `tree/` — holding 24 further `.rs` files, and `grep -rl` for rustix / std::os::unix / termios / libc:: / /dev/tty across all five returns nothing. So the accurate figure is 43 of 46 source files with zero unix references, and the compositor, layout, scroll, selection and tree machinery are all in the clean column.

What follows: the bet — keep pixel-core, replace its tty layer — is resting on a larger and more uniform base than the brief claims for it, which matters because you are weighing that bet against dropping pixel-core and rewriting the browser chrome.

One complication I should state in the same breath, because it bounds the claim: the `engine/` modules do reference `crate::terminal`, but for types rather than syscalls — `engine/doc.rs:6` imports `KeyEvent`, `engine/keys.rs:4` imports `KeyEvent`/`KeyKind`, `engine/input.rs:5` and `engine/embed.rs:5` import `Mouse`/`MouseKind`, and `engine/clipboard.rs:7` imports the `Terminal` struct itself. Those types are defined at terminal.rs:11–121 and are plain data. So the 43 files are portable but not fully decoupled: the seam Task 2 defines has to hand these types out, and `engine/clipboard.rs` is the one call site that wants the concrete `Terminal`. That is an argument that Task 2's instruction to 'derive the trait from terminal.rs's existing callers, not from a fresh design' is the correct instruction rather than boilerplate caution — the callers are enumerable and there are five of them.

What would overturn it: if `engine/clipboard.rs`'s use of the concrete `Terminal` reaches methods that are inherently fd-shaped rather than trait-able, that one module moves out of the free column. I read the import, not the body.
findings.fix: Correct the brief's table to 43 of 46 and add a row naming the five engine/ modules that import terminal.rs types, so Task 2's trait surface is derived from a written list rather than rediscovered.

findings.title: Task 7 is already upstream's default behaviour on Windows — the stock-Electron claim is not a plan, it is the existing code path
findings.body:
The brief argues stock Electron 'should work on Windows unmodified'. Reading the file, it is stronger than that: Windows already gets the right answer with no branch added.

Established from `offscreen.ts`: line 4 is `const SHM_FRAMES = process.platform === "linux" && process.env.TERMINAL_BROWSER_SHM !== "0"`, which is false on Windows. `offscreenPreferences` tests `process.platform === "darwin"` first, which is false, and falls to `{ useSharedTexture: false, useSharedMemory: SHM_FRAMES, deviceScaleFactor }` — i.e. `{useSharedTexture:false, useSharedMemory:false, deviceScaleFactor}`, which is exactly what Task 7's first bullet says to 'add a Windows branch' to return. `initOffscreenMode` throws only under `process.platform === "darwin" && !sharedTextures`, so on Windows it does not throw and logs mode `bitmap` — which is Task 7's second bullet, already satisfied.

Downstream is equally unguarded. `paint.ts:41–43`: `presentPaint` returns `presentTexture` if a texture is present, `presentShmFrame` if an shm frame is present, and otherwise `presentBitmap(surface, image, ...)` with no platform test at all. With both capabilities off, stock Electron's `paint` event supplies only the NativeImage, so `presentBitmap` — `image.toBitmap()` into `surface.present({bgra, width, height, damage})` — is what runs. And the seam is typed for it: `engine/packages/pixel-react/src/surface.ts:8` declares `{ bgra: Buffer; width: number; height: number } & Damaged` as a member of the frame union, routed at line 39 into `engine.updateSurface`.

What follows: Task 7 is not a porting task, it is a confirm-and-test task, and its cost estimate should drop accordingly. More usefully for your risk question, it means the Electron half of the bet needs no new code to be wrong in — the only genuinely new Windows code between Electron and the pane is the backend below `Surface.present`.

Two things I could not confirm, both in the same direction. First, `useSharedMemory` is not in Electron's public offscreen type — the return is cast `as Electron.WebPreferences["offscreen"]` — so it is an upstream-patch key; passing it as `false` to stock Electron should be inert, but I did not run Electron to verify it is ignored rather than rejected. Second, upstream has left a comment on the bgra union member at surface.ts:8 musing about removing that case, so the path the port depends on is one upstream has considered deleting; that bears on re-vendoring, not on whether it works today.
findings.fix: Rescope Task 7 from 'add a Windows branch' to 'assert the existing defaults resolve to bitmap on Windows and lock that in with the per-platform test' — an added branch would be dead code the tests then certify.

findings.title: Nothing else reaches this place: upstream's own tooling excludes Windows and the patched-Electron mirror has no Windows build
findings.body:
The case for acting includes what declining costs, and here declining does not mean 'wait for a better route' — I checked whether one exists.

Established: `scripts/install.sh:9–16` maps only `Darwin-arm64`, `Linux-x86_64|Linux-amd64` and `Linux-aarch64|Linux-arm64`, and everything else exits 1 with 'terminal-browser does not support …'. `scripts/fetch-electron.sh:9–11` offers the same three platforms and pulls from the `zenbu-labs/electron-releases` mirror at line 15. Independently confirmed by grep: there is no `cfg(…windows…)` anywhere in the engine workspace.

What follows: for upstream to reach Windows they would have to build and host a Windows Electron fork they do not currently produce, on top of porting the tty layer — i.e. strictly more work than this plan, which avoids the fork entirely by using the bitmap path. So there is no upstream-will-get-there-eventually option that arrives sooner or cheaper. With WSL ruled out by your framing, the alternative to this plan is not a slower browser in an agwinterm pane; it is no browser in an agwinterm pane.

What this unlocks that is otherwise out of reach is specific rather than general: agwinterm's graphics capability is currently exercised by one static-image producer. A Chromium surface in a pane makes the control-pipe image path a general rendering target, and the plan's own out-of-scope note identifies where that leads — stock Electron on Windows can expose a D3D11 shared-texture handle and agwinterm already renders with Direct2D, so a genuine zero-copy path exists behind this work and behind nothing else.

What would overturn it: upstream announcing or landing Windows support, which I could not check — this review has no network access, and the context directory contains no upstream issue tracker, release notes or roadmap. My evidence is the vendored tree at `.reference/terminal-browser/` as it stands, and it may be behind upstream's HEAD; `docs/design/UPSTREAM.md`, which would pin the commit, is only created at Task 1.

findings.title: pixel-node is already structured for a third platform, and the Owned path it hands Windows is tuned rather than vestigial
findings.body:
Task 6 reads like a porting task; the code suggests it is closer to filling in an existing pattern. Established: `pixel-node/Cargo.toml` puts rustix and libc under `[target.'cfg(target_os = "linux")'.dependencies]`, so the crate has no unconditional unix dependency; `lib.rs:5–12` gates `mod iosurface` on macos and `mod shm` on linux at the declaration, not inside the module. `surface.rs:7–17` defines `SurfacePixels` with `IoSurface` gated to macos, `Shm` gated to linux, and `Owned { bgra, width, height }` ungated — so on Windows the enum has exactly one variant, which is why the plan can say the Windows path 'already exists'.

The part worth knowing beyond that: `Owned` is not an unexercised fallback. `SurfaceMailbox::submit` at surface.rs:53–58 reclaims the dropped frame's `Vec<u8>` into `slot.spare` when a frame is coalesced, and the same buffer-reuse handling appears at lines 101, 125 and 146. Upstream built allocation recycling specifically around the owned-bitmap path. Combined with `BitmapPresenter`'s coalescing in `browser/src/page/paint.ts` — which unions damage rects across dropped frames — the copy path Windows inherits has already had its two obvious costs addressed by someone who cared about frame rate.

What would overturn it, and I want this stated rather than buried: I could not verify that pixel-node builds on Windows, because building is outside this review. Its dependency list includes `openh264 = { version = "0.9.7", features = ["source"] }`, which compiles C++ from source via a build script, plus seven tree-sitter grammars that also build C. Whether those compile under MSVC is unchecked and is a real Task 6 risk that the plan's checklist does not mention; my claim here is about the crate's own platform structure, not about its transitive build.
findings.fix: Add a bullet to Task 6 to build pixel-node's native dependencies (openh264 with the source feature, the tree-sitter grammars) under MSVC before touching draw_frame, so a toolchain problem surfaces as its own finding rather than as a confusing napi failure.

findings.title: The agwinterm half is chartered by agwinterm's own prior design and keeps its justification if winterm-browser stalls
findings.body:
On whether the two-repo split is right: the usual objection to splitting work across repos is that one half is dead weight without the other. That does not apply here, and the evidence predates this port.

Established from agwinterm's own documents: `docs/agterm-gap-analysis.md:41` marks 'Image protocols / graphics' as **Partial** and describes only the out-of-band file path; `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-06-30-agwinterm-design.md:204` records that animation and video-like Kitty frames are 'supported structurally but not the optimization target (docxy emits static images)'. So agwinterm named this exact gap for itself before winterm-browser existed. The dependency plan's own overview lists non-browser consumers — a video preview, an animating plot, a remote frame buffer — and locates the cost correctly ('the expensive part of image.frame is not the placement machinery, which is already good — it is the format and the transport'), which matches what I read in `HandleImageFrame`: the placement and caching machinery is sound and the PNG-file round trip is the only thing being replaced.

What follows: the split places the work in the repository whose own roadmap already wanted it, and the frameshm command is worth building on agwinterm's terms whether or not the browser port completes. That is a different and better reason for the split than 'these are two codebases'.

What would overturn it: if the frameshm layout ends up shaped narrowly around Electron's BGRA paint buffer, the general-purpose justification thins out. The plan's Task 1 header carries per-slot `(width, height, stride, format)` rather than a fixed format, which points the other way, but the spec does not exist yet — `docs/specs/image-frameshm.md` is a Task 1 deliverable and I confirmed it is not on disk today, which is also the thing Task 10's precondition is written to catch.

findings.title: The engine runs in a detached daemon that opens the client's tty by path — a mechanism with no Windows analogue, and no task addresses it
findings.body:
Upstream is a daemon/client split, and the daemon reaches the user's terminal by opening a *path*. I traced the whole chain: `cli/src/main.ts:119` `ownTtyPath()` shells out to the unix `tty` command and keeps the result only if it `startsWith("/dev/")`; `main.ts:301-303` refuses to run without it (`"not running on a tty"`); the path is sent over a unix socket to the daemon, which at `browser/src/daemon.ts:96-106` rejects any open without a `tty` and passes it into `createSession`; `browser/src/session/session.tsx:315` hands it to `createRoot({ tty: this.ctx.tty, ... })`; and `pixel-core/src/terminal.rs:348-349` does `File::options().read(true).write(true).open(tty_path)`. Meanwhile `main.ts:155` spawns the daemon `{ detached: true, stdio: "ignore" }` — it has no console of its own by construction.

On Windows there is no path that names another process's ConPTY. `CONIN$`/`CONOUT$` resolve to the *calling* process's own console, and a detached process has none. `AttachConsole(pid)` is the only handle-across-processes mechanism, it is one-console-per-process, and it attaches to a console the caller does not own.

This is established. What follows from it is that Task 3's design is placed in the wrong process: it says "read from the console input handle" and "enable VT input with `SetConsoleMode`", which assumes the engine owns the user's console. In upstream's architecture the engine is the daemon and never does. The output side is accidentally immune — frames leave out-of-band via the control pipe addressed by `AGWINTERM_SESSION_ID`, so it does not need the tty — which is likely why this never surfaced during design. Input has no such escape: nothing in the 13 tasks proposes forwarding stdin from the CLI client to the daemon, hosting the engine in the foreground process instead, or duplicating a console handle across the boundary. An autonomous executor reaching Task 3 has to invent one of those architectures with no brief to work from.

What would overturn this: evidence that the port intends to abandon the daemon model and run the engine in the foreground CLI process (`createRoot({tty: null})` is a supported shape — `session.tsx:313` has a `!this.ctx.tty` branch). If that is the intent it is a large architectural decision that appears nowhere in the brief or the plan, and it needs to be a task.
findings.fix: Add a task before Task 3 that decides where the engine process lives on Windows and how console input reaches it — foreground-hosted engine, or client-forwards-stdin-over-IPC. Task 3's console work cannot be specified until that is settled.

findings.title: Task 8 cannot launch the browser: the only launcher is the CLI, which Task 11 ports three tasks later
findings.body:
Task 8's first checkbox is "launch Electron OSR". There is exactly one launcher in the tree and it is unported at that point.

`browser/package.json:9` — `"start": "... && exec node ../cli/dist/main.js"`. The CLI is the entry point. `cli/src/main.ts:109` builds the launch command as `return { command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", line], cwd: browserDir };` — every browser launch goes through `/bin/sh`, which does not exist on Windows. Before that, `main.ts:65-68` sets `ELECTRON_DEV_BIN` to `["electron"]` for every non-darwin platform, and `main.ts:83-86` does `fs.existsSync` on it and calls `fail()` if missing — on Windows the artifact is `electron.exe`, so it fails there first. `main.ts:105-108` also wraps arguments in POSIX single-quote escaping and appends `2>>'...'` shell redirection.

That work is Task 11 ("port `cli/src/` entry points: `main.ts`, ..."). So Task 8 — the milestone the goal names as the most valuable thing to get right — sits three tasks before the code that makes it possible. This is established from the two files; what follows is that an autonomous executor at Task 8 either stalls or silently pulls Task 11's work forward, which makes Task 11's later "tests pass" gate meaningless because the code will already be there under a different task's name.

What would overturn this: if Task 8 is meant to bypass the CLI and invoke `electron.exe browser/dist/main.js` by hand as throwaway scaffolding. The plan does not say that, and it would still need the daemon-vs-foreground question above answered first.
findings.fix: Move the `main.ts` launch path (electron binary resolution, spawn without `/bin/sh`) out of Task 11 and into a task before Task 8, leaving Task 11 with the registry/paths/`ssh`/`sandbox`/`upgrade` surface it also covers.

findings.title: Nothing supplies cell pixel metrics on Windows — both of pixel-core's mechanisms are unavailable against agwinterm
findings.body:
Cell size in pixels is what Tasks 5, 8 and 9 all compute against (Task 5: "cell-span computation from pixel size and cell metrics"; Task 9: "the pane's cell metrics, since an off-by-one cell is a wrong click target"). `pixel-core` has exactly two ways to learn it, and on Windows+agwinterm neither works.

`terminal.rs:869-889` `cell_size()`: first `self.size()?.cell_size()`, where `size()` at `terminal.rs:847-855` is `termios::tcgetwinsize` reading `ws_xpixel`/`ws_ypixel`. Windows' `GetConsoleScreenBufferInfo` has no pixel fields — there is no equivalent to report. Second, it writes `b"\x1b[16t"` (`terminal.rs:880`) and waits 300ms for a reply, setting `cell_query_unsupported` on timeout.

agwinterm answers neither. I read its full CSI dispatch at `native/agwinterm-core/src/emulator.rs:964-1045`: the arms are `H f A B C D G d J K X m r L M @ P S T q`, and everything else — including `t` — falls to `HostAction::Unhandled`. There is no XTWINOPS. I also grepped `src/Agwinterm.Pty/ControlServer.cs` for `cell_width`/`CellWidth`/`cell_height`/`CellHeight` and found nothing, so the control pipe does not expose it either, even though agwinterm computes `_cellW`/`_cellH` internally (`src/Agwinterm.App/MainWindow.xaml.cs:225-226`).

Established: both mechanisms are absent. What follows is that `cell_size()` returns `None` on this target, and every pixel↔cell conversion in Tasks 5/8/9 has no input. Note upstream's own herdr fixture (`pixel-core/src/herdr.rs:260`) carries `cell_width_px`/`cell_height_px` in its info payload — upstream solves this by asking the *terminal* over a side channel, which is precisely the mechanism agwinterm's control API does not offer yet.

What would overturn this: an agwinterm control verb or environment variable carrying cell metrics that I failed to find. I searched only for those four identifier spellings in `ControlServer.cs`.
findings.fix: Either add a cell-metrics field to an agwinterm control response (a third repo-crossing contract, so it belongs in the agwinterm plan next to `image.frameshm`), or add `CSI 16 t` to agwinterm's CSI dispatch. Pin it before Task 5, not during it.

findings.title: Mouse input is permanently cell-quantized against agwinterm; the brief's "Input is solved" overstates what the host can deliver
findings.body:
The brief states "**Input is solved** — SGR mouse ... No macOS-style background helper app is needed". The host cannot deliver pointer position better than one cell, and `pixel-core` has an explicit capability flag for exactly this that will read false.

agwinterm's encoder, `src/Agwinterm.Win32/Program.Input.cs:442-453`, computes `int col = ...(pxX - ox) / cw` and `int row = ...(pxY - oy) / ch` and emits `\x1b[<{btn};{col+1};{row+1}M`. Cell integers only — the sub-cell pixel offset is discarded before the sequence is built.

`pixel-core` probes for better: `terminal.rs:361` requests `\x1b[?1016h` (SGR-pixel mouse) at startup, and `terminal.rs:945-948` `probe_mouse_pixels()` sends `\x1b[?1016$p` and waits 150ms for a DECRQM reply. agwinterm has no `1016` anywhere (`emulator.rs:621-623` handles 1002/1003/1006 only), and its DECRQM handler at `emulator.rs:768-774` answers *only* for mode 2026. So the probe times out and `mouse_pixels = false`.

That flag is load-bearing, not cosmetic: `engine/mod.rs:352` sets it from `term.reports_pixel_mouse()`, `engine/pointer.rs:61` gates `let located = self.pixel_mouse.then_some(point)` so hover/pairing get no position, and `engine/scroll.rs:192` gates `wants_cursor` on it.

Established: the encoder, the probe, and agwinterm's lack of 1016. What follows is that a real Chromium browser gets pointer resolution of roughly one cell — upstream's own fixture at `herdr.rs:260` uses 9x19 px cells — so small link targets, hover states, drag-select and scrollbar grabs all quantize. Task 9 does plan a "cell coordinates to page pixels" translation, so the plan encodes the right arithmetic; the objection is that the brief presents this as parity when it is a permanent fidelity ceiling on the headline feature ("a real Chromium browser ... with working keyboard and mouse").

What would overturn this: adding `?1016` support to agwinterm and a pixel-coordinate branch to `SendMouse`. That is a small, well-localized change on the host side — but it is a second agwinterm dependency the plan does not have, and it is not in the agwinterm plan.
findings.fix: Either add `?1016` + pixel coordinates to agwinterm's mouse encoder as a second item in the agwinterm plan, or state the cell-resolution ceiling in the brief so it reads as an accepted cost rather than an oversight.

findings.title: Task 1's `pnpm install` runs the patched-Electron fetch script the plan forbids, via bash
findings.body:
`browser/package.json:7` is `"postinstall": "bash ../scripts/fetch-electron.sh"`.

Task 1 says to run `pnpm install` and record what installs cleanly, and in the same task says "do **not** copy `scripts/` wholesale — `install.sh`, `fetch-electron.sh`, `apparmor.sh` and `bundle.sh` are unix/patched-Electron specific". Those two bullets are in direct conflict: with `scripts/` uncopied, `pnpm install` runs `bash` on a file that is not there; with it copied, it runs the script the Constraints section forbids ("Do not fetch or build a patched Electron"). Either way `pnpm install` fails or does the wrong thing, in the very first task, and the plan presents its outcome as a recording exercise rather than a thing that needs fixing.

This also makes Task 7's premise slightly optimistic. Task 7 correctly identifies `presentBitmap` as a stock-Electron path, but the vendored package still declares `electron: 43.3.0` as a devDependency *and* overrides it at postinstall with the fork. Task 7 never says to delete the postinstall hook, so the fork-fetch stays in the tree as a live install step that Task 12's "verify ... no patched Electron anywhere in the dependency chain" would then have to catch at the end.

Established by reading the manifest. What would overturn it: if `fetch-electron.sh` is a no-op on unrecognized platforms and exits 0 — but it is not copied, so `bash` fails on a missing file regardless, and `bash` itself is not guaranteed present.
findings.fix: Add an explicit Task 1 item: remove the `postinstall` hook from `browser/package.json` and pin the stock `electron` devDependency, recording it as the first intentional divergence from upstream.

findings.title: The two-slot shm design does not make tearing impossible, contrary to the constraint it is written to satisfy
findings.body:
The agwinterm plan states a hard requirement — "Frames must never tear. ... the design must make a torn read impossible, not unlikely" — and its Technical Details claim the two-slot scheme delivers it: "The producer owns one slot at a time and the renderer reads the other. ... A frame in flight is therefore never the frame being read."

That holds only if the consumer never falls more than one frame behind, and nothing in the design gives the producer any way to know whether it has. The producer runs free at Electron's paint rate; the consumer is driven by a control-pipe message that must be received, dispatched through `ControlServer`, and then memcpy an 8 MB 1920x1080 BGRA slot. Concretely: producer publishes seq=1 into slot 0 and sends the message; paints frame 2 into slot 1, publishes seq=2, sends; paints frame 3 and — with only two slots — begins writing slot 0 again. If agwinterm is only now servicing message 1, it copies slot 0 while frame 3 is being written into it. Torn read, and the acquire/release pair on `ready` does not prevent it because the barrier orders the *producer's* publish, not the *consumer's* copy.

What the scheme does guarantee is that a half-written slot is never *published*. That is a different property, and it is the one the Technical Details paragraph actually argues for ("a producer that dies mid-write leaves a half-written slot that is simply never published"). The stated requirement is stronger than what is designed.

The test list does not cover this. Task 3's tests are all argument validation (short view, bad stride, slot out of range, bad name); Task 4's are the `(id, seq)` cache and malformed args. There is no test in which the producer runs ahead of the consumer — the only case where the property under test can fail.

This is reasoned from the plan text, not from code, since the code does not exist yet. What would overturn it: a consumer-side acknowledgement I have missed in the design — but the plan explicitly says "no lock is shared across the process boundary", which rules out the usual mechanisms.
findings.fix: Give the consumer a way to signal the slot it is reading — an in-use word per slot the reader sets and clears, or more slots plus a released-sequence the producer must respect — and add a test where the producer publishes N frames faster than the consumer drains them.

findings.title: The napi build script hardcodes .dylib/.so and will not find the Windows artifact
findings.body:
`engine/packages/pixel-react/scripts/build-native.mjs:9` is `const library = process.platform === "darwin" ? "libpixel_node.dylib" : "libpixel_node.so";`, and line 14 does `fs.copyFileSync(source, destination)` unguarded. `pixel-node`'s manifest declares `crate-type = ["cdylib"]`, which on Windows produces `pixel_node.dll` — no `lib` prefix, different extension. The copy throws ENOENT.

This sits on the critical path for Task 6 ("confirm the napi module loads under Node v22 on Windows") and Task 8 (which needs a built engine), because `pixel-react`'s `build` script is `npm run build:native && tsc`, and `browser`'s `start` script runs `build:engine` first. Neither task mentions this file.

The fix is three lines. The objection is not its size — it is that the plan's Task 6 scopes the Windows work on `pixel-node` entirely to Rust (`SurfacePixels` variants, `draw_frame` match arms), so an executor working that checklist has no reason to look at the JS build script until the build breaks, which is exactly the class of stall that costs a long autonomous run.

Established by reading both files. Nothing would overturn it short of the script being replaced during vendoring, which no task proposes.
findings.fix: Add a Task 6 item covering `build-native.mjs`: platform-select `pixel_node.dll` on win32 and fail with a named path rather than a raw ENOENT.

findings.title: The portability measurement's scope excluded every layer where the port actually breaks
findings.body:
The goal asks whether the reference count is a proxy that fails. Within its own scope it does not fail — I reproduced it exactly. Per-file counts of `rustix::|std::os::unix|termios|libc::|/dev/tty` across `pixel-core/src/*.rs` give 64 for `terminal.rs`, 2 for `herdr.rs`, 2 for `ghostty.rs`, 0 for the other 19. I also checked the 24 files the count never reached — `src/` has 46 `.rs` files, not 22, because `engine/`, `scroll/`, `selection/`, `surfaces/` and `tree/` are subdirectories — and all 24 score zero on the same pattern. On the two dependencies the goal names specifically: `fontdue` is fine (fonts are `include_bytes!`-bundled at `paint.rs:775` and `menu.rs:356`, not loaded from a system font path), and `arboard` is fine (one guarded call site, `clipboard_image.rs:56`, `.ok()?`; `engine/Cargo.lock:27-32` already resolves it to `clipboard-win` on this platform). `rustix` itself builds on Windows — I read `rustix-1.1.4/Cargo.toml:61,238-243` and `src/lib.rs:265,289,301`, where `pipe`/`shm`/`termios` are `#[cfg(not(windows))]` behind a target that is explicitly supported. So `cfg`-gating the source, as Task 2 proposes, is sufficient for `pixel-core`.

The problem is what the measurement was pointed at. It counted Rust identifiers inside one crate, and the brief promotes that to "the port is: replace one module, port one, drop one, keep nineteen" — a claim about the whole port. Every blocker I found is outside the measured region: the tty-by-path daemon architecture lives in `cli/` and `browser/` TypeScript; the `/bin/sh` launcher is `cli/src/main.ts:109`; the `bash` postinstall is `browser/package.json:7`; the `.so` assumption is a `.mjs` build script; the missing cell metrics are a *host* gap, not a guest one. `throttle.rs` — one of the nineteen — is even 60% macOS-only under `cfg`, though it degrades to a no-op cleanly (`supported()` returns `false`) and is not a build problem.

Established: the counts, the file inventory, the three dependency checks. What follows is that the brief's confidence is calibrated to a measurement of the one layer that turned out to be the least risky, and the maintainer is being asked to fund the port on that number.

What would overturn this: it does not overturn the architectural bet itself, which I think survives — keeping `pixel-core` really does look cheaper than dropping it, and the chrome really is untouched. It overturns the *sufficiency* of the evidence offered for it.
findings.fix: Before Task 1, run the same disposition pass over `browser/`, `cli/`, `store/`, `terminals/` and the JS build scripts, and record the result next to the `pixel-core` table so the two halves of the port carry the same standard of evidence.

findings.title: The file-based bring-up path has a read/write race and a staleness hole at frame rate, and its claimed cache benefit is nil for a browser
findings.body:
Task 5 specifies "write it to a temp path" (singular) and "reuse ids across frames so agwinterm's content-signature cache behaves as designed". Reading the consumer, both halves are a problem at video rate.

`ControlServer.cs:451-460` computes `long sig = ContentSignature(path)` and transmits only if it differs from the last accepted signature for that id. `ContentSignature` (`ControlServer.cs:487-496`) is `LastWriteTimeUtc.Ticks ^ (Length << 1) ^ hash(path)` — it never reads the bytes. Two consecutive browser frames written to the same path whose PNGs happen to be the same length, within whatever timestamp granularity the filesystem actually delivers, produce the same signature and the new frame is silently dropped in favour of the cached one. There is no error and no counter that distinguishes it from a legitimately-unchanged frame.

Worse, phase 1 does `ContentSignature(path)` then `File.ReadAllBytes(path)` synchronously while the producer, running free at paint rate, is already writing frame N+1 to that same path. `ReadAllBytes` either hits a sharing violation — caught by the bare `catch { data = null; }` at line 458, which silently degrades to "place the cached image" — or returns a partially-written PNG that the renderer's async decoder then fails on. Task 5 has a bullet for "survive a frame whose file write fails"; it has none for the read side, and the plan never specifies a unique path per frame or an atomic rename.

Separately, the stated rationale is inverted. The content-signature cache exists to skip re-transmits of *unchanged* images. A browser frame differs every frame, so the cache never skips, and "reuse ids across frames so the cache behaves as designed" buys nothing — every frame pays a full stat, a full file read, a PNG encode upstream and an async PNG decode downstream (`ControlServer.cs:474` hardcodes `KittyFormat.Png`). That matters because Task 8's frame-budget measurement is "the case for the shm path", and the plan describes the file path as a reasonable bring-up floor rather than as something that may be too slow to demonstrate the milestone at all.

The cache mechanics and the `catch` are established from the code. The race and the timestamp collision are reasoned from it — I did not measure NTFS `LastWriteTime` update granularity or attempt a concurrent read, and I could not, since the producer does not exist yet.

What would overturn this: writing each frame to a unique path, or `File.Move`-ing into place atomically, closes both holes — but then the id-reuse cache genuinely never fires, since `hash(path)` is in the signature.
findings.fix: Specify unique-path-per-frame (or atomic rename) in Task 5, drop the id-reuse rationale, and add cleanup of the resulting file churn to the existing temp-file bullet.

findings.title: The brief and the agwinterm plan already describe different `image.frameshm` wire shapes, and the brief is the document the plan tells you to read first
findings.body:
The goal asks whether the contract between the repos is pinned. Two documents currently describe it and they do not agree.

The brief's transport diagram (`docs/design/00-port-brief.md:124`) shows `{"cmd":"image.frameshm","args":{"handle":..,"w":..,"h":..}}` — a **handle**, flat args, `w`/`h`. The agwinterm plan's Task 1 defines `{"images":[{"id":N,"name":"Local\\...","slot":N,"seq":N,"width":N,"height":N,"stride":N,"format":N,"row":N,"col":N,"cols":N,"rows":N}]}` — a **name**, an images array mirroring `image.frame`, and `width`/`height`. Different field names, different nesting, and a materially different mechanism: passing a `HANDLE` across processes needs `DuplicateHandle` against the target process; passing a `Local\` name needs neither. The agwinterm plan's design is the coherent one; the brief's is the stale one, and the Windows plan's own Overview instructs the reader to "Read it first — it records what was measured rather than assumed".

A second field is unpinned even in the good version: the agwinterm plan's Task 3 says "restrict accepted names to a fixed prefix in the `Local\` namespace" without ever stating the prefix, and the Windows plan's Task 10 says "create the named mapping" without one. Neither document contains the string a producer must actually use.

The Windows plan's Task 10 precondition — that `docs/specs/image-frameshm.md` exists — is the right instinct and mitigates most of this. But that spec is also where the agwinterm plan's Task 6 writes its throughput measurement, so the file exists and is authoritative from agwinterm Task 1 while remaining incomplete until agwinterm Task 6. "The spec file exists" is a weaker gate than it reads.

Established by reading both documents side by side.
findings.fix: Correct the brief's diagram to the `images[]`/`name` shape now, before either plan starts, and state the literal `Local\` prefix in the agwinterm plan's Task 1 so both sides code against the same string.

findings.title: Every mode negotiation and query reply pixel-core relies on crosses ConPTY's input translation, which agwinterm's own source documents as lossy
findings.body:
The brief treats the ConPTY boundary as lossy in one direction only — "ConPTY strips APC" — and calls the other direction solved: "Input arrives *through* the pty as ordinary VT sequences ... so it needs no side channel". The input direction is also a translation layer, not a byte pipe, and agwinterm's own code says so about a neighbouring case.

`native/agwinterm-core/src/emulator.rs:1052-1056` carries this comment about OSC 9;9: "*Crucially this is the cwd form that conhost/ConPTY passes THROUGH to the client (it swallows OSC 7), so under a pty-host it is the only way the live cwd reaches the terminal-side emulator.*" That is a documented instance of ConPTY dropping a sequence that is not APC, discovered the hard way in this codebase.

Everything agwinterm sends the child goes through that path: `src/Agwinterm.Win32/Program.Sessions.cs:290` is `public void Respond(string reply) { ...; _s.Write(...); } // query reply -> PTY`, the same `Write` that `SendMouse` uses. So the DECRQM replies pixel-core waits on (`\x1b[?1016;1$y`), the `CSI 16 t` cell-size report, and kitty-keyboard CSI-u reports are all synthesized host-side and pushed into the ConPTY input pipe for conhost to reinterpret before the child sees them.

I established the mechanism — that these all cross the translation layer, and that the layer is known to drop things here. I did **not** establish that any specific sequence fails; I could not, since running the port is what would show that. The plausibility argument cuts both ways: agwinterm 0.17.2 is in daily use, so basic SGR mouse evidently survives for ordinary apps. Kitty keyboard reports and `$y` DECRQM replies are far more exotic and are exactly what `pixel-core` depends on.

The reason this bears on the decision at all is placement: the earliest task that would expose it is Task 9, after the Task 8 milestone has been declared reached. A cheap check — send one DECRQM through a Debug agwinterm to a child in VT-input mode and see what arrives — costs an hour and de-risks Tasks 3 and 9 both.

What would overturn it: that check coming back clean.
findings.fix: Add a probe to Task 1's baseline: from a child under a Debug agwinterm with `ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT` set, record the exact bytes received for an SGR mouse report, a kitty-keyboard CSI-u report, and a DECRQM `$y` reply. Record it next to the `cargo check` baseline.

findings.title: pixel-node pulls openh264 with the `source` feature — an unverified C++ build on the Task 2 and Task 6 critical path
findings.body:
`engine/crates/pixel-node/Cargo.toml:26` is `openh264 = { version = "0.9.7", features = ["source"] }`. The `source` feature builds the vendored OpenH264 C/C++ sources through a build script rather than linking a prebuilt library. Task 6 scopes the Windows work on `pixel-node` entirely to Rust surface variants and `draw_frame` match arms and does not mention it; nor do `tree-sitter` (six grammars, all C) or `mp4`.

This also touches Task 2, whose stated deliverable is "`cargo check --workspace` is clean on Windows". `cargo check` still runs build scripts, so a build-script failure in `openh264-sys2` would make Task 2's gate unreachable for a reason that has nothing to do with the tty seam it is actually testing.

I want to be exact about what I did and did not do here: I read the manifest, which is established. I did **not** attempt the build — the review is read-only and I was asked not to run builds — so I do not know whether it compiles under the MSVC toolchain on this machine. I am reporting it because the plan's task decomposition assumes `pixel-node`'s Windows risk is entirely in the Rust it names, and there are three C/C++ dependencies it does not name. It may well build fine, in which case this costs nothing to have checked.

What would overturn it: `cargo check -p pixel-node` succeeding on this machine, which Task 1's baseline run would reveal anyway if its error list is recorded per-crate rather than only for `pixel-core`.
findings.fix: Have Task 1's baseline record `cargo check` results per crate, not just `pixel-core`, so a `pixel-node` build-script failure is visible before Task 2 depends on a clean workspace check.

text: 12 findings

findings.title: agwinterm never encodes kitty keyboard on the input side — "agwinterm emits both" is false for keyboard
findings.body:
Task 3 states "decode SGR mouse reports (?1006) and kitty keyboard sequences — agwinterm emits both, so the work is consuming them, not negotiating them", and the brief (docs/design/00-port-brief.md:57-60) generalises this to "Input is solved". I traced the host side and the keyboard half does not exist.

Established by reading: agwinterm's only key encoder is `OnKeyDown` at C:/Users/boris/source/agwinterm/src/Agwinterm.App/MainWindow.xaml.cs:636-695. It is a legacy VT table — `\x1b[1;<mod>A` for arrows, `\x1bOP` for F1, `\r`, `\x7f`. It never reads `KeyboardFlags` (exposed at Agwinterm.Core/ITerminalCore.cs:38) and emits no CSI-u form anywhere; I grepped `src` and `native` for a CSI-u/key-encode path and found none. `kitty_keyboard` (native/agwinterm-core/src/emulator.rs:805-815) and `keyboard_flags()` (:293) only parse the client's DECSET and answer its query — agwinterm acknowledges the protocol it does not speak. Concretely: no key-release events, no event-type field, no repeat distinction; `Ctrl+A..Z` collapses to a control byte at MainWindow.xaml.cs:651-657 so Ctrl+Shift+X is indistinguishable from Ctrl+X; and Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+T/N/W are intercepted for agwinterm's own UI at :643-646 and never reach the client at all — Ctrl+Shift+T is the browser's reopen-closed-tab.

What follows from that (my inference): Task 9 is under-scoped by a feature that lives in the *other* repository, and this is a second cross-repo dependency that the plan does not record. Constraint line 54-58 pins only the frameshm contract.

The project's own record agrees, in your words. agwinterm's docs/windows-terminal-gap-analysis.md:61 lists "win32-input-mode / Kitty keyboard protocol | CSI ? 9001 h | **Missing** | M". Issue yeroo/agwinterm#98 ("VT protocol audit", your own, closed) has an unchecked box reading "`?9001` win32-input-mode — ConPTY asks us for Windows Terminal's enhanced key encoding. Honoring it (**encode keys as win32-input-mode records when on**) improves key fidelity through conhost." That issue also shows the same parse-but-don't-emit pattern for `?1004` focus reporting, so this is a documented class rather than one oversight. On the close: #98 has zero comments and was closed within nine seconds of #105 and #91, so it is a bulk close carrying no reasoning — it records that the gap was scoped, not that it was declined.

One thing would overturn this: if legacy VT keys are good enough for the browsing you actually intend, key-up and Ctrl+Shift being unavailable is a quality ceiling rather than a blocker, and Task 9 stands as written.
findings.fix: Either add a task (here or in agwinterm) to implement host-side key encoding — kitty CSI-u or win32-input-mode per #98 — and record it as the second pinned cross-repo dependency alongside frameshm; or restate Task 3/Task 9 and the brief's "Input is solved" to say keyboard is legacy-VT fidelity only, and state what that costs.

findings.title: Nothing in the 13 tasks installs or launches Electron on Windows; Task 8 is blocked from both ends
findings.body:
Goal item 3 asks whether the Task 8 milestone is reachable where it sits. It is not, for two reasons that both sit outside Task 8.

**Task 1 aborts.** browser/package.json:7 is `"postinstall": "bash ../scripts/fetch-electron.sh"`. Task 1 (docs/plans/20260821-windows-port.md:102-103) explicitly does *not* copy `scripts/`, naming `fetch-electron.sh`. So the postinstall points at a file that will not exist. Even if it were copied, scripts/fetch-electron.sh:8-13 is a `uname` case that ends `*) echo "fetch-electron: unsupported platform"; exit 1`. Either way `pnpm install` — Task 1's own checklist item at :106 — fails on the browser package rather than producing the "which packages install cleanly" record it asks for. No task in the plan removes or replaces that postinstall.

**Task 8's launcher is deferred to Task 11.** cli/src/main.ts is what spawns Electron (browser/package.json:10 `"start": "... exec node ../cli/dist/main.js"`). `electronBinary()` at cli/src/main.ts:74-78 resolves `browser/node_modules/electron/dist/` + `ELECTRON_DEV_BIN`, which is `["electron"]` on every non-darwin platform (:65-68). On Windows that file is `electron.exe`, so `browserLaunchCommand`'s `fs.existsSync` guard at :80-86 fails and reports `missing … — build the browser first`, which is the wrong diagnosis. cli/src/main.ts is Task 11 (:241-252), three tasks after Task 8 (:198-210).

Worth stating because it cuts the other way: `"electron": "43.3.0"` is a plain devDependency at browser/package.json:22. So stock Electron for Windows does arrive through an ordinary install once the postinstall is neutralised — the no-patched-Electron premise is better grounded than the brief argues, and the missing piece is plumbing, not architecture.

Established by reading; I did not run `pnpm install` (this review is read-only) and node_modules is not present, so the `.exe` suffix is from the electron package's standard Windows layout rather than from disk. Two things would overturn it: pnpm being configured to skip the workspace project's own postinstall, or Task 8 being understood as licence to improvise a launcher rather than use the CLI.
findings.fix: Add to Task 1: drop or Windows-guard browser/package.json's postinstall so `pnpm install` completes on stock Electron. Move the `electronBinary()`/`ELECTRON_DEV_BIN` `.exe` fix out of Task 11 into a task before Task 8, or state in Task 8 that it launches Electron directly and defers the CLI.

findings.title: Task 2 cannot meet its own deliverable: terminal.rs holds the crate's input-type vocabulary, imported by 12 of the untouchable 19
findings.body:
Task 2 says "move the existing unix implementation behind `#[cfg(unix)]`" (:120-121) and names its real deliverable as "`cargo check --workspace` is clean on Windows" (:126). Those two bullets are in tension, because terminal.rs is not only a tty layer.

Established by reading: terminal.rs is 2617 lines and defines the crate's whole input vocabulary in the same file as the termios/shm/pipe code — `Event` (:11), `KeyEvent` (:26), `KeyKind` (:49), `Mods` (:57), `Key` (:65), `Mouse` (:94), `MouseKind` (:103), `MouseButton` (:114), `TerminalColors` (:122), `ColorSlot` (:139), `WindowSize` (:175), `Terminal` (:227), `Waker` (:304), `SessionEnv` (:315). Twelve other files import `crate::terminal::*`, and they are in the keep-unchanged column: engine/keys.rs (`KeyEvent`, `KeyKind`, and ~30 `Key::` arms), engine/doc.rs, engine/input.rs (`Mouse`), engine/embed.rs (`Mouse`, `MouseKind`), engine/clipboard.rs (`Terminal`), native.rs (`Waker`).

What follows (my inference, from Rust semantics): `#[cfg(unix)]` on the module removes those types on Windows and all twelve fail to compile, so the task's deliverable is unreachable by its own recipe. The alternative — lifting the types into a portable module — means editing the `use` lines in those twelve files, which collides with the constraint at :63-64 ("Do not weaken the 19 keep-unchanged modules") and would be flagged by Task 12's `git diff` check at :260-261.

There is a clean route the plan does not name: keep terminal.rs present on Windows as a facade that `pub use`s the portable types and gates only the impl. An executor following the bullet literally will not find it before breaking twelve modules.

Overturned if ralphex is expected to redesign around checklist bullets rather than follow them.
findings.fix: Split Task 2 explicitly: first extract the portable types (Event/Key/KeyEvent/Mods/Mouse/WindowSize/Waker/SessionEnv) into their own module and re-export from `terminal` so the 12 importers are untouched; only then cfg-gate the unix impl. Say so in the bullet, and note in Task 12 that a re-export shim is the expected diff.

findings.title: The brief and the agwinterm plan disagree on the shm wire shape — `handle` versus a named mapping
findings.body:
Goal item 4 asks whether the contract between the two repos is actually pinned. On the one field that crosses the process boundary, the two documents say different things.

The brief — which scope.md:7 calls "the authoritative design" and the plan at :8-9 says to read first — shows `{"cmd":"image.frameshm","args":{"handle":..,"w":..,"h":..}}`. The agwinterm plan defines the args as `{"images":[{"id","name":"Local\\...","slot","seq","width","height","stride","format","row","col","cols","rows"}]}` (context/agwinterm-dependency-plan.md:103-105) and opens the mapping with `MemoryMappedFile.OpenExisting(name, MemoryMappedFileRights.Read)` (:126).

These are not two spellings of one design. A Win32 HANDLE is process-local; its numeric value means nothing in the consumer unless the producer calls `DuplicateHandle` into the consumer's process, which requires knowing the consumer's PID and holding rights to it. The named-mapping shape is the workable one — so the brief is the wrong document here, and it is the document the plan tells the executor to trust. The Windows plan's own Task 10 (:229-232) says "create the named mapping", so the plan is right and the brief is stale; a reader who follows the plan's instruction to read the brief first gets the wrong shape.

A second gap in the same area, less certain: agwinterm's reader will "restrict accepted names to a fixed prefix in the `Local\` namespace" (dependency plan :130-131). The Windows plan's Task 10 never mentions a required prefix. If the exact prefix is not written into docs/specs/image-frameshm.md at agwinterm Task 1, the producer picks a name and is rejected at runtime with a validation error that looks like a bug.

Established by reading both documents; the DuplicateHandle point is Win32 semantics, not something I tested. Overturned if `handle` in the brief was always shorthand for the mapping name — in which case the fix is a word, but the word matters because ralphex codes against it.
findings.fix: Correct the brief's diagram to the named-mapping args before Task 10 starts rather than at Task 13, and add the exact `Local\` name prefix to the agwinterm Task 1 spec bullet so both sides pin the same string.

findings.title: Two slots plus an unsynchronised copying consumer does not make a torn read impossible
findings.body:
The dependency plan sets itself a hard constraint at :48-50: "Frames must never tear. A producer writing while the renderer reads is the default failure mode of any shared buffer; the design must make a torn read impossible, not unlikely." Its Technical Details at :198-203 then claims the two-slot scheme achieves that: "A frame in flight is therefore never the frame being read."

That claim does not hold for two slots without a back-channel. The consumer copies from the slot named by `ready`; nothing tells the producer when that copy finishes. Trace it: consumer reads `ready`=5 (slot A) and begins its memcpy. Producer fills slot B, publishes `ready`=6. Producer — free-running at browser paint rate, which is the entire premise — now needs a slot for its next frame, and the only other slot is A. It fills A while the consumer is still copying A. Torn read. A 1920x1080 BGRA frame is ~8 MB per copy, so the window is not narrow, and the failure gets *more* likely exactly when the producer is fast, which is the case the command exists for.

This is analysis of a written protocol, not of code — none exists yet — which is why my confidence is not higher. But the header already carries a slot count (:100-102), so the fix is cheap: three or more slots, or a consumer-written "currently reading" index the producer skips. It has to land in agwinterm Task 1, because the Windows plan's Task 10 (docs/plans/20260821-windows-port.md:229-231, "write BGRA into the inactive slot") codes against whatever that spec says, and "the inactive slot" is only well-defined if there is exactly one.

Overturned if the producer is to block until the consumer acknowledges, or is rate-limited below consumer speed by construction — neither is stated anywhere in either plan.
findings.fix: In agwinterm Task 1, either raise the slot count to three or add a consumer-published `reading` index to the header, and correct the Technical Details paragraph so the stated invariant matches the mechanism.

findings.title: Nothing sources the cell metrics and pane pixel size that Tasks 5, 8 and 9 all require
findings.body:
Task 5 requires "cell-span computation from pixel size and cell metrics" (:169-170), Task 9 requires a translation that "accounts for deviceScaleFactor and the pane's cell metrics" (:217-218), and Task 8 must render Chromium at some pixel size. I looked for where those numbers come from on Windows and found no supported source.

Established by reading: agwinterm's session-targeted control dispatch is `session.write/type/text/status` and `image.show/sixel/clear/frame` (ControlServer.cs:242-249). Grepping ControlServer.cs for `cell_width`/`cellW`/`CellSize`/`PixelWidth` returns nothing; `_cellW`/`_cellH` live only in Agwinterm.App/MainWindow.xaml.cs:700 and are not exposed through the pipe. Grepping all of `src` and `native` for XTWINOPS (`14t`/`16t`/`18t`) returns nothing, so the client cannot ask the terminal for its pixel size either. Task 3's resize source (:139, console screen buffer info) yields cols and rows in character cells only.

The project's own record makes the query route worse, not better: issue yeroo/agwinterm#98 records, from a live VT tap, that "DSR/CPR (`CSI 6n`), DA1/DA2 — conhost responds on our behalf", and that an OSC 8 sent from a pane never reached the emulator. So a `CSI 14t` from inside a pane is likely to be answered by conhost or swallowed, never reaching agwinterm.

A workaround exists and the brief half-implies it: `image.frame` takes `cols`/`rows` (ControlServer.cs:444-445) and agwinterm scales the image to that cell span, so the producer can render at any resolution and let the terminal resample. But that costs text sharpness on a browser, and it is not what the plan says it will do. Either way this is potentially a third thing agwinterm must expose, alongside frameshm and key encoding.

Overturned if you intend to hardcode or configure cell metrics for v1, which would be reasonable — but the plan should say so, because an autonomous executor will otherwise go looking for a query that does not exist.
findings.fix: Decide and record where cell metrics come from — a new control verb, a config value, or "render at fixed resolution and let cols/rows scale it" — and add it to Task 4's client surface before Task 5 needs it.

findings.title: Mouse position is quantised to one character cell; there is no pixel-resolution mouse anywhere
findings.body:
Task 9 warns that "an off-by-one cell is a wrong click target", which frames the risk as translation accuracy. The real constraint is coarser: correct translation still lands the pointer on a lattice.

Established by reading: `SendMouse` at C:/Users/boris/source/agwinterm/src/Agwinterm.App/MainWindow.xaml.cs:710-720 takes `(col,row)` from `CellAt` (:700), which is integer division of the pointer position by `_cellW`/`_cellH`, and emits `\x1b[<btn;col+1;row+1M`. Sub-cell position is discarded before the sequence is built, so it is not recoverable downstream by any amount of care in the port. `?1016` (SGR-Pixels) appears nowhere in agwinterm's `src` or `native` — I grepped for it and got nothing — and the emulator's mode handler covers only 1000/1002/1003/1006 (TerminalEmulator.cs:402-405). The brief's own quoted herdr metrics put a cell at 9x19 px.

What follows (my inference): in Chromium, every click, hover and drag snaps to a ~9x19 px grid. Hovering a 12 px link, placing a text caret mid-word, dragging a scrollbar or a column divider all become imprecise in a way no code in this repo can fix. That is a fair amount of "a real Chromium browser" (Overview, :5-6).

This is separate from the keyboard finding above and has a separate fix, which is why it is listed on its own. Overturned if cell-granularity pointing is acceptable for the intended use — plausible for reading and navigating, less so for the "page with a text input" and "heavy page" cases in Post-Completion (:294).
findings.fix: Either accept and record cell-granularity pointing as a known limitation in the brief and Task 9, or add `?1016` SGR-Pixels to agwinterm and to the pinned cross-repo dependency list.

findings.title: The zero-hit column contains modules that compile clean and silently behave differently on Windows
findings.body:
Goal item 1 asks whether the unix-reference count is a failing proxy, and names arboard and fontdue. I checked. The count itself is sound; the proxy does fail, in a specific and narrow way.

**Confirmed first, so you know what I cleared.** The 64/2/2 split and "19 of 22 with none" reproduce exactly. The "22 source files" counts only top-level modules — `pixel-core/src` actually holds 46 `.rs` files across `engine/`, `scroll/`, `selection/`, `surfaces/`, `tree/` — and re-running the same pattern over those 24 extra files returns zero hits, so widening the sample strengthens rather than weakens the claim. fontdue is genuinely free: every font is `include_bytes!("../../../assets/fonts/JetBrainsMono-Regular.ttf")` (paint.rs:775, menu.rs:356, text_input.rs:917, wrap.rs:139, tree/tests.rs:8), `engine/assets/fonts/` is a real directory and not a symlink, so there is no system font discovery to port — the usual Windows font-porting tax does not apply. arboard is used at exactly one call site (clipboard_image.rs:56) and is declared `arboard = { version = "3.6", features = ["wayland-data-control"] }` at engine/Cargo.toml:20; that feature gates a Linux-only optional dependency, which cargo excludes for a Windows target. I read this rather than building it, so it is the one item here I would still want a `cargo check` to confirm. native.rs degrades safely rather than breaking: `helper_path()` (native.rs:83-87) returns `None` without `NATIVE_SCROLL_HELPER`, so dropping upstream's Swift helper costs precise scroll and pinch-zoom, not a build.

**Where the proxy fails.** clipboard_image.rs:88-92 has zero unix-API references, compiles clean on Windows, and does the wrong thing: it rejects any path not starting with `/` or `~`, so `C:\Users\...` and `file:///C:/Users/...` both return `None`, and it resolves `~/` through `std::env::var("HOME")`, which Windows does not set. Pasting or dropping a file into the browser silently no-ops with no error path. Second instance: throttle.rs:71-73, `CpuThrottle::supported()` returns `cfg!(target_os = "macos")`, so the CPU throttle is inert on Windows; it is re-exported at lib.rs:58 and used by engine/mod.rs:40. That matters for Task 8's frame-budget measurement (:206), which will be taken with frame pacing that exists on macOS simply absent.

Both sit in the keep-unchanged 19, so fixing either collides with the constraint at :63-64 and Task 12's diff check at :260-261 — the same collision as the Task 2 finding, reached from a different direction. Overturned if clipboard file-paste and CPU throttling are both out of scope for v1, which is defensible but is currently unstated.
findings.fix: Add to Task 1's ➕ findings: clipboard_image.rs needs Windows path acceptance and USERPROFILE, and throttle.rs is inert on Windows. Record both as sanctioned exceptions to "keep 19 unchanged" now, so Task 12's diff check does not treat them as violations.

findings.title: Precedent: adding a control verb is a well-worn, repeatedly-accepted shape here, and the conformance constraint is now a CI gate
findings.body:
Reporting the sweep result so silence is not read as "no precedent exists". winterm-browser has no remote and three local commits, so there is no forge history for this repo; I swept agwinterm's, which has one (yeroo/agwinterm) with `gh` available.

**Supports the transport decision.** Adding a verb to the control API is routine and has been accepted repeatedly on its merits: #7 `feat(control): session.rename verb` (MERGED), #8 `feat(control): session.seen, sidebar read-back, version in ping` (MERGED), #68 `feat(control): font can target a specific split/scratch/quick pane` (MERGED), #201 `feat(control): resolve a session target by name, not just by id` (MERGED, 2026-08-20). `image.frame` itself was built for an external consumer, docxy, and is described in docs/agterm-gap-analysis.md:41 as delivered "out-of-band because ConPTY strips APC". So `image.frameshm` is not a novel shape for this project — it is the fourth or fifth instance of one it keeps choosing, for a reason that still holds.

**Strengthens the conformance constraint.** PR #195 `test(control-api): make the cross-product contract a gate` was merged 2026-08-18, three days before these plans. The dependency plan's rule at :43-46 — do not add `image.frameshm` to tests/conformance/control-api.json — is therefore not caution about a shared file, it is a recently-enforced CI gate that would fail agliteterm's build. That constraint is correctly stated and should not be softened during execution.

**Does not bear.** Upstream terminal-browser has no recorded position on Windows: README.md, AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md mention neither Windows, Win32 nor WSL. scripts/install.sh:9-14 refuses non-Darwin/Linux, which the brief cites correctly, but that is a packaging fact rather than a decision anyone argued.

I have anchored this on plan line 58 only because it is the constraint the precedent bears on; the line itself also carries a small error, below.

findings.title: The shm-contract precondition is stated against Task 9 but consumed at Task 10
findings.body:
Constraints line 54-58 reads "If the contract is not ready when Task 9 starts, stop and say so rather than inventing a shape." The contract is not consumed at Task 9 — Task 9 is Interactive input (:212-222) and touches no shared memory. The precondition belongs to Task 10, which states it correctly itself at :226-227.

Established by reading the two task bodies. It matters only because of how these plans are executed: an autonomous runner reading the Constraints block literally can halt at the top of Task 9 for a missing precondition Task 9 does not need, and "stop and say so" is exactly the instruction it would follow. The same sentence also says "Everything up to and including the first-frame-on-screen milestone uses the file-based image.frame", which is right and identifies Task 8 as the boundary — so the off-by-one is in the task number alone.

Overturned if Task 9 was meant to be the number after a renumbering, in which case the whole block wants re-reading against the current task list.
findings.fix: Change "when Task 9 starts" to "when Task 10 starts" in the Constraints block.
